opus-5.5.text:
I think it's the rational thing to do. If you're an entrepreneur and the money is available on attractive terms, you raise it, because you know that money won't always be there. That's how bubbles work. I've studied them over a long time, and there's a very consistent pattern: great new technologies produce real excitement, the excitement brings in a flood of capital, prices get ahead of the cash flows that can realistically support them, and eventually the need for cash collides with the reality of what those assets produce. Then the credit tightens and a lot of people who looked brilliant get wiped out.

But it's important to separate two things: the technology and the investment. The railroads changed the world. So did the internet. Yet many of the people who invested in them at the peak lost a great deal of money. Believing that AI will be transformative, which I do, doesn't mean every AI company, or every price being paid for one, makes sense. Both things can be true at the same time.

So when I see an entrepreneur raising a lot of capital now, I interpret it as buying insurance. The money gets them through the period when funding dries up, and the ones left standing with cash can survive, and even buy assets cheaply from those who didn't prepare. That's what a good entrepreneur should do. It doesn't necessarily mean they think their own company is overvalued, although the fact that they're eager to sell shares at these prices tells you something. They're on the other side of that trade.

What usually pricks a bubble isn't people realizing the technology doesn't work. It's a need for cash: debts have to be serviced, taxes have to be paid, or central banks tighten, and people have to sell assets to get money. Wealth on paper isn't money you can spend, and when everybody tries to convert one into the other at the same time, that's when you get the break.

So the lesson for the entrepreneur is to raise the money, but don't let it make you fragile. Don't build a cost structure that requires the next round to come at a higher price. And the lesson for the investor on the other side is to ask whether the price you're paying can be justified by future cash flows, and how you'd be positioned if you're wrong. It comes down to surviving the bad scenario, because the ones who survive get to enjoy the transformation that follows.

r001.rationale: It says the AI entrepreneur is raising capital by selling shares, which communicates adding AI company shares to the market.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that if I were an AI entrepreneur and I believed there was a bubble, raising a lot of capital now would be exactly the smart thing to do. That's not a contradiction, that's good sense. When money is cheap and abundant, you take it. The question isn't whether to raise, it's what you do with it.

Let me explain how I think about bubbles, because I've studied them going back hundreds of years. A bubble has a pretty consistent set of ingredients. Prices are high relative to traditional measures of value. People are pricing in rapid future growth that may or may not materialize. There's broad bullish sentiment, so everyone's optimistic. Purchases are being financed with a lot of leverage. New buyers are coming into the market who weren't there before. And there's this feeling that it's different this time. When I look at the AI space right now, I'd say a number of those boxes are checked. Not all of them, but enough that I'd call it bubble-like.

But here's the thing people get wrong. A bubble doesn't mean the underlying technology isn't real. In the 1920s, the automobile and the radio were genuinely transformative, and there was a bubble. In the late nineties, the internet was genuinely transformative, and there was a bubble. The dot-com bust wiped out most of the companies, but it didn't wipe out the internet. Amazon survived. The ones that survived were the ones that had cash and real economics when the music stopped.

So when I see an entrepreneur raising ahead of a possible bursting, I ask two things. First, are they raising to build something that generates real value, or are they raising because they can and they're going to spend it on acquiring customers at a loss forever? Second, do they understand the environment they're operating in? Do they know that the liquidity that's flooding in today can disappear very quickly, and that when it does, the companies that survive are the ones with runway and discipline?

Think about it like this. Raising capital in a bubble is like filling your boat with supplies before a storm. If you're smart, you take on provisions and you stay disciplined, and when the storm comes, you're one of the few boats still floating while everyone else is bailing water. If you're foolish, you take the supplies and you throw a party on deck.

And there's a bigger picture here that I'd add. We're in a moment where there's an enormous amount of money chasing a limited number of ideas. That happens late in long-term debt cycles when there's a lot of liquidity sloshing around. The central banks created a lot of money, and that money has to go somewhere. So part of what you're seeing in AI valuations isn't just about AI. It's about the amount of money in the system looking for a home.

So my interpretation of an entrepreneur raising capital ahead of a bubble bursting is, if they're doing it with their eyes open, it's wisdom. If they're doing it without understanding where they are in the cycle, it's going to end the way it always does. The difference is whether they know which game they're playing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses raising capital and how to use it, but does not say that this increases the supply of AI stock.

astra-6.text:
I would separate two questions: Is the technology transformative, and is the investment worth the price? Those are very different questions. You can have a technology that changes the world and still have a bubble in the companies developing it.

If you’re an entrepreneur and investors are willing to give you capital on attractive terms, raising it can be sensible. You’re building a cushion so that, if financing dries up, you can continue operating. That doesn’t necessarily mean you believe the bubble is about to burst.

The important question is what you do with that money. Are you building something that can ultimately produce enough earnings to justify the investment? Or does your business depend on somebody continually giving you more money? When the enthusiasm fades, that distinction becomes very important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses raising capital as a cushion for the entrepreneur, but does not say this increases the supply of AI stock.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would separate two things: whether AI is going to change the world, and whether the investments in AI will produce good returns at the prices being paid. Those are very different questions. You can have a transformative technology and still have a bubble.

If you’re an entrepreneur and capital is available on attractive terms, raising it can be sensible. You’re giving yourself the ability to keep operating if financing dries up. That doesn’t necessarily mean you know when a bubble will burst. It means you recognize that the availability of money changes.

Then the question is: what do you do with that money? Can you build a business that generates enough cash to sustain itself? Because when the enthusiasm goes away, that’s what matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an entrepreneur raising capital to keep operating, but does not say this increases the supply of AI stock.
